title: Open his eyes (2 Kings 6:15–17)
hookLine: the servant sees enemy armies; Elisha prays and the hills are full of fire

lines: ALAS, MY MASTER! HOW SHALL WE DO?
cards: Early morning in a town called Dothan. Elisha's young servant gets up before his master, opens the door, and steps outside.
The hills are covered: horses, chariots, a whole army from the king of Syria, sent overnight to capture the man asleep inside.
Elisha has been warning the king of Israel where the Syrians would lie in wait, not once nor twice, and the Syrian king has had enough.
The servant runs back in, and the King James Bible keeps his words exactly as a frightened person says them: "Alas, my master! how shall we do?"

teach.h: THEY THAT BE WITH US ARE MORE.
teach.b: Elisha doesn't say the army isn't there. He says: "Fear not: for they that be with us are more than they that be with them." Two men in a house, cavalry outside, and his count comes out in their favor.
Then he prays, and notice what he asks for. Not an escape. Not fire from heaven.
"LORD, I pray thee, open his eyes, that he may see."

teach.h: A PRAYER FOR SIGHT, NOT ESCAPE.
teach.b: The prayer isn't for the situation to change, but for the servant's sight. "The LORD opened the eyes of the young man; and he saw: and, behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha."
The fire was already there. Then the story turns. The Syrians come down, and Elisha prays the opposite: that the soldiers be struck blind.
He leads the confused army into the capital, Samaria, and when their eyes open, the king of Israel wants to strike them down. Elisha says no: set bread and water before them.
So the king throws them a great feast and sends them home, and the chapter says the raiding bands of Syria came no more into the land of Israel. Christians read this scene in more than one way.
Some hear it about angels, a help that is real but usually unseen. Others hear a picture of faith itself: not seeing new things, but seeing the same hillside differently.
Either way, the hinge is a three-word prayer for someone else.

how: Some Christians turn to Elisha's servant at Dothan in frightening seasons, and some pray Elisha's request, open his eyes, for someone who is afraid; the scene is also read in churches when teaching about angels and unseen help.

games.q: you're Elisha. your servant runs in shaking: an army has surrounded the town to take you. what do you do?
o: slip out the back before they come in.
pray that your servant's eyes would be opened.
call down fire on the army.
games.why: "LORD, I pray thee, open his eyes, that he may see." the young man looks again and the mountain is full of chariots of fire.

practice: Bring to mind the thing that feels like an army on the hill right now, and let it be as big as it is.
Then start a second count, slowly: a friend, a sister, a neighbor, a doctor, someone who prayed for you without saying so, a strength you forgot to list.
If you pray, you can borrow Elisha's words for someone else, open his eyes, or open her eyes; if you don't, just keep counting quietly.

wordCard.voice: Dothan. The town where Elisha's frightened servant saw the hills full of horses and chariots of fire, after a prayer: open his eyes.

orig.note: Hebrew: open (the eyes), the verb of Elisha's prayer in 2 Kings 6:17.

carryVoice: Your line: more with us. The hillside never changed; the seeing did. That's plenty for today.
